definition: The powers or presences honoured in Shinto, which may be associated with natural features, ancestors, places or exceptional people. The word is often translated as 'god' or 'spirit', but kami are not all-powerful and are approached with respect rather than worship in the strict sense.

The Japanese tradition of honouring kami at shrines through offerings, purification and festivals. The term covers a wide family of local practices rather than a single organised religion with one founder or scripture.

Japan's oldest surviving chronicle, presented to the court in 712 CE and combining myths, songs and imperial genealogy. It was compiled partly to legitimise imperial rule, yet it preserves older stories and variant details.

The court's official history, completed in 720 CE, which recounts the same myths as the Kojiki but often gives several versions side by side. It is a key source for early Japanese religion and statecraft.
The shadowy land of the dead to which Izanami went and which Izanagi tried to leave behind. It is pictured as a polluted realm separated from the living by a great boulder.
The gate, usually of wood or stone, that marks the entrance to a shrine's sacred ground. Passing through it is understood as a move from ordinary space into a place set apart for the kami.
Rites of purification that remove pollution and restore a clean state before approaching a kami. Izanagi's bath after returning from Yomi is often cited as an early model for such purification.

A curved, comma-shaped bead made of stone, jade or other precious material, used in necklaces and offerings. Strings of magatama appear among the treasures given to Ninigi and in the story of the cave.
The 'grass-cutter' sword that Susanoo found in one of the serpent's tails and sent up to Amaterasu. It became one of the three sacred treasures of the imperial line.
A festival in which a local kami is honoured with offerings, music, processions and shared food. Matsuri keep the stories and the shrine community alive from year to year.
